• Name: Marron crayfish
  • Scientific name: Cherax tenuimanus / Cherax cainii
  • Other names: Hairy Marron / Smooth marron
  • Minimum tank size: 130 gallons (~500 litres)
  • Breeding: Easy-Medium
  • Diet: Omnivore
  • Temperament: Aggressive
  • Life span: up to 10 years
  • Colour: Brown

Cherax tenuimanus (Hairy marron or Margaret River marron) is endemic to the Margaret River in southwestern Australia. It is naturally restricted: it is known from only eleven sites along a section of the Margaret River and occurs in an area less than 50 km in length.

Cherax cainii (Smooth marron) occurs over much of the south-west of Western Australia (as far east as Esperance and as far north as Geraldton), where it forms the basis of a popular recreational fishery and aquaculture industry. More recently it was introduced into South Africa, Zimbabwe, Japan, the USA, China and the Caribbean as a commercial aquaculture species.

These crayfish prefer clear, fast-flowing streams and rivers with sandy bottoms and abundant vegetation. The water is soft, acidic and high in tannins.

In natural habitats, cool, flowing, well-oxygenated water allows marron to thrive, while they tend to avoid stagnant backwaters. Ideal marron habitat consists of freshwater environments with plentiful vegetation, woody debris, rocky banks and muddy substrates that let them easily meet their cover and dietary needs.

The minimum recommended tank size for one Marron crayfish is 130 gallons (500 litres). A pair (male and female) will require at least 40 gallons (120 litres). These crayfish grow huge. A larger tank is always preferable for the stability of water chemistry and makes it easier to create diverse hiding areas.

  • Too many crayfish in insufficient space leads to increased aggression, injuries and cannibalism. Overcrowding is the main source of stress for crayfish, particularly with more than one male, as males are more aggressive than females.
  • Long tanks are better than tall tanks of the same size for any crayfish species. Unlike fish, they mostly need room to crawl from side to side, not up and down.
  • Crayfish are very good escape artists. Covering the tank is absolutely necessary. They are strong enough to move the lid, so make sure it is stable.

All crustaceans have a hard, multi-layered exoskeleton that does not grow with the animal, so marron must moult as they grow. Calcium (Ca) is an essential component of the exoskeleton, and growing a new one requires a lot of calcium for calcification. Moulting leaves them vulnerable.

When about to moult, marron become less active, stop eating and seek shelter. Otherwise they can easily fall prey to tankmates.

• Temperature: The ideal range is 68–75°F (20–24°C). Although they tolerate low temperatures, they stop growing below 55°F (12.5°C). Growth also declines rapidly above 75°F (24°C), with mortality at 86°F (30°C) and above.
  • pH: 7.0–9.0.
  • Hardness: They appreciate hard water, GH 8–20.
  • Oxygen: Dissolved oxygen should be kept at or above 6 mg/L. They become stressed when levels drop below 3 mg/L. They need good aeration and water flow.
  • Salinity: Experiments showed that marron may tolerate, although not necessarily reproduce in, salinities from 0 to 15 ppt. Growth decreases above 6–8 ppt.

Filters

No special requirements. Any filter that suits the size of the tank will do. However, sponge filters can be a bad idea, as the crayfish like to chip and chew on them and will eventually shred the sponge.

Lighting

No special requirements. They are nocturnal animals and used to live with very little light. If you have plants or other animals in the tank, adapt the lighting to their needs.

Substrate

No special requirements. These crayfish are not diggers.

Decorations

Decorations provide shelter for crayfish, so the more decorations, the happier they will be. They appreciate all types of leaves, rocks, driftwood, PVC pipes, etc.

These crayfish are omnivorous scavengers, feeding on both plant and animal matter. They are not picky and will eat a wide variety of food: aquatic plants, decaying vegetation, dead or decaying organic matter, algae, small insects, insect larvae, worms, snails, crustaceans, tadpoles, frogs, fish eggs/fry, etc. They are opportunistic feeders and adjust their diet to food availability.

Studies suggest that for optimal growth they require a diet of 30–40 percent protein, at 10–15% of body weight per week (about 2% of body weight per day if fed daily). Since this is hard to calculate, it is enough if the food does not exceed the size of the carapace.

In aquariums, suggested foods include leaves, plants, blanched vegetables, crushed snails, earthworms, dead fish or shrimp, bloodworms, detritus worms, tubifex worms, blackworms, etc.

  • Diet type: Omnivorous
  • Food preference: Mix of meat and vegetation
  • Feeding frequency: 3–4 times a week for adults; daily for juveniles

Feeding rules

  • Schedule: Feed before lights out.
  • Leave food for 24 hours before removing it. To prevent water contamination, siphon out leftovers before adding fresh food. Leaves can stay in the tank for several days.
  • Leave old exoskeletons: Do not remove moulted exoskeletons, to improve health.
  • Check hiding places: Marron often drag and store food in their hiding spots for later, so check them from time to time to prevent bacterial contamination.
  • Crayfish need variety. Do not give the same food all the time; change the diet periodically.

Marron crayfish are crepuscular or nocturnal and most active just after sunset. During the day they tend to stay hidden under logs, rocks and debris. They are not social and generally do not share hiding spots; for the most part they are solitary.

They can be aggressive toward each other and other crayfish, especially when defending territory, competing for food or during mating. Males in particular fight using their large front claws. When threatened, they can move rapidly backward by curling and unfolding the abdomen.

Marron are a non-burrowing species; instead of digging deep tunnels they prefer to live under shelter.

  • Social: No
  • Active: No
  • Peaceful: No
  • Territorial: Yes
  • Burrowers: No

Tankmates

Keeping marron with other crayfish species or even conspecifics is not recommended, for two reasons: they grow really big, and they will eventually fight, with more aggressive species becoming dominant.

They can also be hostile to fish, crabs, dwarf frogs and especially freshwater snails. Bottom-dwelling, slow-moving or long-finned fish (like Betta) will be the first to get hurt.

Plants

Marron are not compatible with live plants. Like most crayfish, they will try to eat, cut, shred and uproot everything in the tank, so planted tanks are not recommended. The only viable options are plastic plants, floating plants and some cheap plants you are ready to lose.
The male deposits a spermatophore between the female's 5th pair of legs.

Cherax cainii grows slightly faster than Cherax tenuimanus and is more readily bred, including in captivity. The two species can successfully hybridize.

  • Maturity: At least 2 to 3 years, at a total body length of 3.1–4.3 inches (8–11 cm).
  • Mating: The eggs take nearly half a year to develop inside the female. The male deposits a spermatophore between the female's 5th pair of legs.
  • Eggs: On average, females incubate 200–400 eggs for 12–16 weeks on the pleopods under the tail (large females may produce up to 800), from which about 150–250 juveniles are released.
  • Hatching: Newly hatched young cannot live separately from the mother for a further 2–4 weeks. They need to moult before becoming fully independent. Females whose young have become independent should be separated from females still carrying eggs or young to prevent cannibalism.

Note: Two types of crayfish share the name "Marron crayfish". Despite being closely related and similar both physiologically and genetically, to the extent of potential hybridization, Cherax cainii has proven more successful and better adapted to survival. Cherax tenuimanus is currently listed as rare under the Western Australian Wildlife Conservation Act 1950 and is managed as 'critically endangered' (according to IUCN criteria) by the Western Australian Government (CALM 2005).

Taxonomy

In 1912, Cherax tenuimanus was first described as a single species by G.W. Smith. Several subsequent studies of Cherax taxonomy also referred to only a single species.

In the 1980s, another closely related crayfish was discovered in the same region. Based on differences in electrophoretic and morphological characteristics, Marron crayfish were split into two subspecies, and this classification was maintained in subsequent studies.

In 2002, the new subspecies was elevated to species based on a review of allozyme data and was given the name Cherax cainii.

Etymology

The generic name Cherax is thought to derive from the Greek "Kherax", meaning "a kind of lobster" or "crayfish". It may also be a misspelling of the Greek "charax", meaning a pointed stake or a thing that scratches, referring to the sharp, pointed rostrum and spiny claws.

The species name "Tenuimanus" combines the Latin "tenuis" (thin or slender) and "manus" (hand or limb), referring to the slender, thin claws (chelipeds) of this crayfish compared with others in the genus Cherax.

Description

  • Size: One of the largest crayfish species in the world, growing to more than 15 inches (38 cm) in total length and recorded at more than 4.4 lb (2 kg). Smooth marron can grow to 60–150 g in 12 months and 100–300 g in 24 months.
  • Carapace: Hairy marron have a median carina that extends continuously, without depression, to the cervical groove, prominent tufts of long recumbent setae, and no tuberculation on the areola compared with Smooth marron.
  • Telson: Marron are easily distinguished from all other Cherax species because they are considerably larger and have spines on the telson.
  • Colour: Generally dark marron, good camouflage in southern waters rich in brown tannins. An electric blue variety is now raised for aquariums, and an orange striped marron was recently found in the south-west.

Lifespan

Some reports indicate they may live over 10 years in optimal tank conditions. In nature, lifespan is affected by predation, disease and environmental factors.
